lead: Through these days the first reading follows the story of Abraham. Today God calls Abram to leave his country, his kindred and his father’s house, and promises that in him all the families of the earth shall be blessed; Abram goes, building altars as he travels. In the Gospel Jesus warns against judging others and tells us to take the log out of our own eye first. On the memorial of St Aloysius Gonzaga, a young man who left a prince’s inheritance to follow Christ, Psalm 33 sings: “Happy is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he has chosen as his heritage.”

r.h: Go to the land that I will show you
set: The first eleven chapters of Genesis end with the tower of Babel, where humanity is scattered and divided. Then comes the family of Terah. Abram, with his wife Sarai, who has no child (11:30), has moved with his father from Ur of the Chaldeans to Haran in northern Mesopotamia (11:31). Here God speaks to him. With this call the history of salvation takes a new turn: God begins to heal the whole human family through one man and his descendants.

Abram’s route runs south through Canaan, through places that will matter greatly in Israel’s story: Shechem, Bethel and the Negeb, the dry south. At each stop he builds an altar. He owns nothing in the land yet; he claims it only by worship.
str: vv. 1–3: God’s call and promise: land, a great nation, blessing, a great name, and blessing for all the families of the earth.
vv. 4–5: Abram goes, at seventy-five, with Sarai, Lot and all they have.
vv. 6–7: at Shechem the Lord appears and promises the land to his offspring; an altar.
vv. 8–9: near Bethel another altar; Abram calls on the name of the Lord and journeys on toward the Negeb.
kw: Literally “go for yourself” or “go by yourself”. The call asks Abram to leave, in three widening circles, his land, his clan and his father’s household. He is told where to leave, but not yet where he will arrive: “the land that I will show you”.

Words from the root “bless” come five times in vv. 2–3. Some commentators note that the story of sin in chapters 3–11 is marked by curses; now the story of salvation begins with blessing, and it is meant for “all the families of the earth”.
The land is promised to Abram’s “offspring” (v. 7). St Paul notes that the word is singular, and reads it of Christ, in whom the promise is fulfilled (Galatians 3:16).
vv: Go from your country and your kindred and your father’s house to the land that I will show you.
Faith begins with a word from God and a road whose end is not yet seen.
and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
Abram is chosen not for himself alone but for the sake of all peoples. Paul calls this verse the gospel proclaimed beforehand to Abraham (Galatians 3:8).
So Abram went, as the Lord had told him;
No speech, no question: only obedience. The Letter to the Hebrews sums it up: “By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called… not knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8).
ch: The Catechism teaches that, in order to gather together scattered humanity, God calls Abram from his country, his kindred and his father’s house, and makes him Abraham, the father of a multitude of nations (CCC 59). The people descended from him were to be the trustee of the promise (CCC 60). The Letter to the Hebrews lays special emphasis on Abraham’s faith (CCC 145), and the Church calls him our father in faith. Christians share this root with the Jewish people, to whom the promises first belong and whose calling God does not revoke (Romans 11:29).

r.h: First take the log out of your own eye
set: The Sermon on the Mount now turns to how disciples treat one another. Jesus has taught the Lord’s Prayer, with its petition to forgive as we are forgiven (6:12). Here he forbids the judging that condemns. He does not forbid all judgment: a few verses later he asks his disciples to recognise false prophets by their fruits (7:15–20). What he forbids is the harsh, self-righteous verdict on another person’s heart. A saying of Hillel in the Mishnah teaches something similar: do not judge your neighbour until you have stood in his place.
str: vv. 1–2: do not judge; the measure you give will be the measure you get.
vv. 3–4: the speck in your neighbour’s eye and the log in your own.
v. 5: “You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye.”
kw: Here it means to pass sentence, to condemn. “That you may not be judged” is a way of speaking of God’s judgment without naming God.
A speck of chaff or sawdust against a roof beam. Jesus, the carpenter’s son, uses a deliberately comic picture: a man with a beam in his eye offering to do eye surgery on his brother.
In Greek the word meant an actor, one who plays a part behind a mask. The one who judges harshly is playing the part of the righteous man.
vv: Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.
Not a ban on telling right from wrong, but on taking God’s place as judge of another person.
and the measure you give will be the measure you get.
The picture is of a market measure for grain. The mercy we show others is the measure we ask God to use for us.
You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your neighbor’s eye.
Jesus does not say we should never help our brother. He says: begin with yourself. Only a humble eye sees clearly enough to help.
ch: The Catechism names rash judgment as a sin against truth and the good name of others: assuming a neighbour’s moral fault without enough foundation (CCC 2477). To avoid it, it quotes St Ignatius of Loyola: every good Christian ought to be more ready to give a favourable interpretation to another’s statement than to condemn it (CCC 2478, in substance). Examination of conscience and the sacrament of penance are the Church’s way of taking the log out of our own eye.

qa: If we must not judge, how can parents or the Church correct anyone?

Jesus forbids condemning another person’s heart, not caring about right and wrong. Correction given in love is a work of mercy; Jesus himself teaches how to correct a brother (Matthew 18:15). The difference lies in the eye and the heart: the one who corrects well has first looked at his own faults, speaks humbly, and wants his brother’s good, not his own victory.
rite: St Aloysius Gonzaga (1568–1591) was the eldest son of the Marquis of Castiglione in northern Italy, and was raised to be a soldier and a prince. While still a boy he resolved to give himself to God. Against his father’s strong opposition he renounced his inheritance in favour of his brother and entered the Society of Jesus in Rome in 1585. His spiritual director was St Robert Bellarmine. In 1591 plague struck Rome, and Aloysius nursed the sick in the hospitals, carrying the dying in his own arms. He caught the disease and died on 21 June, at the age of twenty-three. The Church honours him as a patron of young people. Like Abram, he left his father’s house for a land God would show him.
study: Abram went “not knowing where he was going”. Where is God asking me to take a step of trust before I can see the end of the road?
Whom have I judged harshly in recent days? What might the “log” in my own eye be?
